etymology: Also bothsidesism: the studio graph with two guests, as though the shape of the panel were the shape of the evidence.
committed_when: One position is supported by the evidence and the other by its existence.
tell: The two sides get the same airtime, and the audience infers the same standing.
counter: Ask what the evidence weighs, not what the panel looks like. Balance is about who gets heard; accuracy is about what is true.
senses: Presenting two sides as equally supported when the evidence is lopsided, because a balanced panel feels fairer than an accurate one.

It works because fairness is a real journalistic virtue and symmetry looks like it. But a coin that lands heads ninety times out of a hundred is not evenly disputed, and equal time misrepresents it as such.
example: *"Some say the bridge is safe, others say it will fall."* One of those groups has the inspection report.

confused_with.tell: Equivalence says the two claims are alike; false balance gives them alike treatment and lets the audience draw the first conclusion.
